subject: Biology
title: Mycorrhizal Networks
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mycorrhizal Networks.

hook.text: Beneath a forest floor, fungi and tree roots form a vast network scientists call the 'Wood Wide Web.'

buildup.text: Mycorrhizal fungi wrap around roots and trade minerals for sugars the tree produces.

discovery.text: Trees share nutrients through this fungal network—mother trees send sugar to struggling seedlings.

twist.text: Some plants cheat—they tap the network for resources without giving anything back.

climax.text: About 90% of plant species depend on mycorrhizal partnerships to survive.

punchline.text: Forests are connected underground by fungi.

quiz.question: What do mycorrhizal fungi trade with tree roots?

details.summary: Mycorrhizal fungi form underground networks connecting plant roots across entire forests, enabling nutrient exchange between trees. These fungal networks transport carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus between plants, with large mother trees supporting seedlings through shared resources.
details.whyItMatters: Mycorrhizal networks reveal forests as cooperative systems rather than collections of competing individuals. Disrupting these networks through soil disturbance or deforestation can collapse forest ecosystems far beyond the immediate damage site.
takeaways: About 90 percent of land plants form mycorrhizal partnerships with fungi
Mother trees share carbon and nutrients with seedlings through fungal networks
The networks have been popularly called the wood wide web

faq.question: How do mycorrhizal networks actually work?
faq.answer: Fungal threads called hyphae connect to plant roots, extending far beyond what roots alone could reach. The fungus provides water, phosphorus, and nitrogen from soil in exchange for carbon sugars from the plant. These threads link multiple plants creating underground nutrient highways.

faq.question: Can trees really communicate through fungal networks?
faq.answer: Trees transfer carbon and chemical signals through mycorrhizal connections. Injured trees release defense compounds that travel through the network, potentially warning neighbors. Whether this constitutes true communication is debated, but the resource sharing is well documented.
